summary: Defines GMPLS routing and signaling extensions for networks in which routers take part in several different data plane switching layers or regions under one control plane. This is the multi-layer and multi-region network (MLN/MRN) case. It builds on the existing GMPLS framework.

plainLanguage.summary: Imagine one traffic office directing cars, trains, and boats at once. This explains how a single control system can manage a network that has several different kinds of switching.

questions: what is a hybrid node in gmpls
what is a virtual te link
what is a soft forwarding adjacency
subtitle: How one GMPLS control plane can run a network that mixes packet, time-slot, wavelength and fiber switching.

tldr.problem: Some networks mix several switching technologies, such as packet and TDM or wavelength, under one GMPLS control plane, but plain GMPLS cannot describe the internal adjustment between them, pick which switching capability a path uses, or advertise links that are not yet built.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6001 adds an Interface Adjustment Capability Descriptor to OSPF and IS-IS, a Switching Capability subobject and a Label subobject for the RSVP-TE exclude route object, and two ways to set up virtual TE links: call-based edge-to-edge association and Soft Forwarding Adjacencies.
tldr.outcome: A single control plane instance can plan and signal paths across several layers or regions inside one TE domain. It is a Proposed Standard and updates six earlier RFCs.

today: RFC 6001 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2010. The metadata lists no obsoleting or updating RFC. It updates RFC 4202, RFC 4203, RFC 4206, RFC 4874, RFC 4974 and RFC 5307.

sections.title: Multi-Layer and Multi-Region Networks
sections.content:
GMPLS (RFC 3945) extends MPLS to several switching types: packet (PSC), Layer 2 (L2SC), time-division multiplexing (TDM), wavelength (LSC) and fiber (FSC). A switching type identifies an LSP region, as defined in RFC 4206. A network with several switching types under one GMPLS control plane instance is a Multi-Region Network (MRN).

A data plane layer is a set of network resources that can terminate or switch traffic of one format. LSC, TDM VC-11 and TDM VC-4-64c are three different layers. A network whose nodes take part in several such layers under one control plane instance is a Multi-Layer Network (MLN).

The RFC covers one control plane instance serving one, two or more layers inside a single TE domain, meaning a group of LSRs that enforce a common TE policy. Several control plane instances serving separate sets of layers are out of scope. The rationale and requirements come from RFC 5212, and RFC 5339 evaluates them against GMPLS.
sections.plainLanguage: Some networks speak several 'languages' of switching at once, like a harbor with trucks, trains and ships. This RFC helps one boss control all of them together.

sections.title: What Needed Extending
sections.content:
Per RFC 5339, most MLN/MRN requirements depend on local procedures, policies or TE algorithms that sit outside the GMPLS protocols, so they need no protocol changes. Four areas do need extensions:

  • Routing: advertising the internal adjustment capability of hybrid nodes.
  • Signaling: constraining multi-region paths by including or excluding switching capabilities. An XRO Label subobject is also added, because RFC 4874 lacked one.
  • Signaling: setting up and deleting virtual TE links.
  • Routing and signaling: graceful TE link deletion.

This RFC handles the first three, in Sections 3, 4 and 5. The fourth is handled in RFC 5710, with extra context in RFC 5817.
sections.plainLanguage: Most jobs in a mixed network can be done with what already exists. Only a few new tools were missing, and this RFC builds three of the four.

sections.title: Advertising Adjustment Capability
sections.content:
A hybrid node has at least one interface that supports more than one switching capability. Inside it, distinct switching elements are joined by internal links. These links have finite capacity, and that capacity MUST be taken into account when computing the path of a multi-region TE-LSP.

For example, a node with PSC and LSC capability can switch a wavelength LSP, but cannot terminate it if no adjustment capability between the LSC and PSC parts is free. So nodes need to advertise the adjustment capability to terminate LSPs, not just the interface switching capability. The RFC adds the Interface Adjustment Capability Descriptor (IACD) for this. It does not change the existing Interface Switching Capability Descriptor from RFC 4202.

In OSPF the IACD is an optional sub-TLV of the TE Link TLV, with Type 25 and variable length. In IS-IS it is an optional sub-TLV of the Extended IS Reachability TLV, with Type 27, in the same format. Multiple IACD sub-TLVs MAY appear in one TE Link TLV.

The IACD carries a Lower Switching Capability and Lower Encoding, an Upper Switching Capability and Upper Encoding (set to 0xFF when the upper capability has no access to the wire), eight Max LSP Bandwidth values for priorities 0 to 7 in IEEE floating point (bytes per second), and a variable field reserved for future technology-specific data. The bandwidth values show the resources still available for insertion and extraction at each priority. Different adjustment capabilities at the two ends of a TE link are allowed.
sections.plainLanguage: A hybrid node is like a loading dock where a truck's cargo moves onto a train. Before sending cargo there, you want to know if a free crane is left. The IACD is the sign that tells you.

sections.title: Multi-Region Signaling
sections.content:
Under RFC 4206, a node at a region edge checks the ERO to find where the region ends, then looks for an existing Forwarding Adjacency LSP (FA-LSP) that matches, has enough unreserved bandwidth and has a compatible G-PID. If none exists, it sets up a new one. In an MRN this can lead to single-hop FA-LSPs between each pair of nodes. When a TE link advertises several switching capabilities, an ERO cannot say which one to use.

To fix this, the RFC defines a Switching Capability subobject (Type 35) for the EXCLUDE_ROUTE object (XRO) of RFC 4874. It names a switching capability to exclude on a given link. Including a capability is done by excluding the others, so to include LSC, a sender excludes PSC, L2SC, TDM and FSC. The design keeps exclusions in the XRO and inclusions in the ERO.

The SC subobject is 4 bytes long. Its L bit is 0 when the attribute MUST be excluded and 1 when it SHOULD be avoided. It MUST follow the interface subobject it refers to. The RFC also adds a Label subobject (Type 3) to the XRO, encoded like the ERO Label subobject of RFC 3473 except for the L bit. It MUST follow the interface subobjects it refers to and, when both are present, the SC subobject. Its label values then MUST be compatible with the excluded capability.
sections.plainLanguage: If a loading dock offers both a train and a boat, the old directions could not say which to use. Now you can say 'not the boat', and the network picks the train.

sections.title: Virtual TE Links
sections.content:
A virtual TE link is a TE link between two upper-layer nodes that has no fully provisioned FA-LSP in a lower layer. It is advertised like any TE link, within an IGP area, and stands for the chance to set up an FA-LSP later. Two techniques are given.

Edge-to-edge association needs no state on transit LSRs. It extends the RSVP-TE Call procedure of RFC 4974: the two end nodes, which MUST be in the same LSP region, exchange identification and TE attributes through a call. The result fills the local TEDB and is advertised as a TE link. When an upper-layer LSP uses it, FA-LSPs MUST be set up to make the link real. A new CALL_ATTRIBUTES object (class 202) carries Call Attributes TLVs. TLV Type 1 holds flags, and bit 0, the Call Inheritance Flag, MUST be 1 to turn the association into a TE link advertisement (the default). Setting it to 0 hides the link or withdraws its advertisement, and the matching FA-LSP SHOULD be torn down. The Notify message MUST also carry an LSP_TUNNEL_INTERFACE_ID object.

A Soft Forwarding Adjacency (Soft FA) sets up the FA LSP in the control plane without committing data plane resources. It can be done with pre-planned LSPs or with path-provisioned LSPs that request zero bandwidth. The new Pre-Planned LSP flag (bit 6 of the Attributes Flags TLV from RFC 5420) is 0 for a fully provisioned LSP and 1 for control plane only. Re-signaling the same LSP with the flag at 0 commits the resources. Zero-bandwidth provisioning is straightforward for packet and L2SC LSPs. For TDM and LSC, a NULL label value prevents data plane allocation, and actual labels are exchanged on commitment.
sections.plainLanguage: A virtual link is a bridge you have drawn on the map before building it. Either both ends agree on it with a phone call, or you reserve the bridge on paper only, and pour the concrete when someone needs to cross.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility
sections.content: The new objects and procedures run inside one TE domain with a consistent TE policy, which the RFC does not specify. Edge LSRs MUST be able to process Call Attributes if edge-to-edge association is used, and intermediate LSRs are transparent to call processing. An LSR that does not support the CALL_ATTRIBUTES object forwards it unexamined and unchanged. If Soft FA is used, both edge and intermediate LSRs MUST support the LSP ATTRIBUTE object processing described above.
sections.plainLanguage: The new tools work inside one company's network. Nodes in the middle can just pass the new notes along without reading them.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC adds no new security considerations beyond those in RFC 5920, because the extensions apply within a single TE domain under one administrative authority. Call initiation, however, MUST stay under the control of the TE domain administrator. Edge nodes MUST keep their call controller unreachable from external TE domains, and security associations MUST be established between the edge nodes that start and end calls, using IKE (RFC 5996) for mutual authentication.
sections.plainLanguage: Only the network's own staff may start these calls, and the two ends must prove who they are to each other first.

sections.title: IANA Assignments
sections.content:
IANA created the RSVP class CALL_ATTRIBUTES (202, C-Type 1), a Call Attributes TLV registry (Type 1 is the Flags TLV, 0 is reserved) and a Call Attributes Flags registry (bit 0, Call Inheritance Flag). It added the Pre-Planned LSP flag (bit 6) to the Attributes Flags TLV and two EXCLUDE_ROUTE subobjects: Label (3) and Switching Capability (35).

For routing, the IACD is OSPF TE link sub-TLV 25 and IS-IS sub-TLV 27.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA is the official list keeper. It wrote down the new numbers so nobody reuses them for something else.

fields.name: L
fields.desc: 0 means MUST be excluded; 1 means SHOULD be avoided.

fields.name: Attribute
fields.desc: 0 is reserved; 1 means the SC is excluded or avoided on the preceding interface.

fields.name: Switching Cap
fields.desc: The switching capability value to exclude.

items.title: IACD
items.text: Routing sub-TLV that advertises how a hybrid node adjusts between switching capabilities.

items.title: XRO subobjects
items.text: Switching Capability and Label subobjects to exclude capabilities and labels during signaling.

items.title: Virtual TE links
items.text: Edge-to-edge calls or Soft FAs advertise links before FA-LSPs carry traffic.
